6739: Habitat modification is a leading driver of species loss. However, following habitat modification not all species decline and the ecological mechanism underlying these differences remains uncertain. One intuitive means to explain which species are lost is species’ niche to environment matching. If species niche requirements are unavailable or reduced in a modified habitat, this should lead to reduced abundance or local extinction. Species affiliation with vegetative strata may be a critical axis limiting species in modified habitats, due to the extensive simplification of vegetative structure following habitat conversion. Using 34 studies of anuran community composition, we evaluate the role of vertical niche position in defining abundance within primary forest, plantation, and pastures. We test the hypothesis that species that use higher vegetative strata will be most severely reduced following conversion of tropical forest, and that this reduction will be most severe in structurally simple pastures. Our results confirm that vertical niche position is an important predictor of abundance in modified habitats. Yet surprisingly we show that abundance in modified habitats increases with vertical niche position, such that arboreal species are more dominant in modified habitats than terrestrial species. This counterintuitive result could come about because physiological tolerance to desiccation and high temperatures experienced in forest canopies pre-adapt these species to the harsher abiotic conditions in pasture. What limits a species’ ability to persist is not always clear. Structural components of a species’ vertical niche may be less important than other traits correlated with vertical niche position.

We found evidence for variable ecological responses to reserve protection among several species. The biomass of the targeted Chrysophrys auratus (snapper) and Cheilodactylus spectabilis (red moki) was significantly greater within Leigh marine reserve in 2018 compared to 1978, and in 2018 reserve sites compared to non-reserve sites. We describe several negative responses to protection, including lower biomass and density of the non-targeted Notolabrus celidotus (spotty) in Leigh, perhaps in response to predator recovery. We also present results indicating a long-term decline in Parapercis colias (blue cod) biomass and density, but positive effects of reserve protection in 2018. Overall, we report complex, variable responses to reserve protection within northeastern New Zealand’s reef fish communities.
6746: Managing the cumulative effects that arise from natural and human stressors is one of the most pressing and complex problems facing coastal and marine decision-makers today. Cumulative effects management is particularly complicated by: fragmented legislative regimes and institutions that cannot account for cross-scale interactions; chronic data scarcity and high levels of uncertainty making system-based assessments and predictions difficult; and conflicting societal and economic expectations, values, and rights that are inadequately integrated into decision-making processes. Without effective processes, models, and political will, decision-makers struggle to implement management strategies that effectively tackle cumulative effects. Emerging efforts to address cumulative effects in Aotearoa New Zealand and Australia provide an opportunity to assess the efficacy of various management strategies operating at different scales and in different legislative and cultural contexts. This research uses primarily qualitative methodologies (literature reviews, interviews, focus groups, and workshops) to compare work in Australia to implement the Reef 2050 Plan, and preliminary attempts in Aotearoa NZ to develop national scale cumulative effects management frameworks and principles. The work undertaken in Aotearoa NZ is intended to be trialled and implemented through the ecosystem-based management initiatives of the Sustainable Seas National Science Challenge.

6747: Many elasmobranch species display a degree of site affinity in relation to foraging, mating and birthing. The reef manta ray, Mobula alfredi, appears to display a strong affinity to cleaning stations – structural features that host a variety of small teleost fishes that remove ectoparasites and necrotic tissue – however, there is a paucity of data in relation to this aspect of their ecology. This study used a VEMCO Positioning System (VPS) that was installed at an aggregation site for M. alfredi at Lady Elliot Island on the Great Barrier Reef. The array of acoustic listening stations triangulated the position of tagged manta rays to provide detailed information about the movements of individuals through space and time. Additionally, in-water surveys of animal behaviour, counts of cleaner fish abundance and diversity, and detailed mapping of the structure of the site were conducted. Over the course of a year, the VPS determined 13,107 positions for 34 tagged animals. Within the array, rays appeared to spend the majority of their time at locations identified by surveys as high-use cleaning stations. This finding supports the hypothesis that M. alfredi aggregation sites may be related to quality cleaning station habitat.

6748: The Māori world view is defined by whakapapa – the story of how each person connects to their world through one big cosmic geneology which their ancestors gifted to them. In this world each is responsible to look after their environment for the generations to come. The Māori values of utu, manaakitanga, wairuatanga and karakia, among others, offer an alternative to the western separation of people from nature and the take make waste practices that have led to environmental crises.
Office of the Māori Climate Change Commissioner
6749: Marine natural products are increasingly becoming sought after as leads for drugs and drug-like compounds with a broadening range of allied commercial applications, especially in the agrichemical sector. Anti-tumour active compounds Halichondrin B and Peluroside A from New Zealand sponges; Salicylihalamide A and Lobatamide A from a Western Australian sponge and an ascidian, are prime examples. These have been generated from hypothesis driven discovery programs where knowledge of the chemical ecology of encrusting invertebrates has refined collection protocols. Analysis of Australasian biomedicinal data derived from marine collection campaigns, suggests that the greatest proportion of useful leads have come from marine invertebrates that are known to aggressively compete for space, or that have biochemical mechanisms that permit settlement and growth ‘over’ other space occupying species. Hence it is not surprising to find that sedentary marine invasive invertebrates are well equipped with a chemical arsenal for ensuring occupation of territory. This arsenal is built from a flexible and sophisticated biochemistry, aided and abetted by ‘selected’ micro-organisms. We describe the chemical ecology of marine invertebrate species that out-compete others and provide insight into why marine invasive species do so well.
6750: Seabed 2030 is a collaborative project between the Nippon Foundation and GEBCO, which aims to bring together all available bathymetric data to produce the definitive map of the world ocean floor by 2030 and make it available to all. To date, the Seabed 2030 Project increased the percentage of the ocean floor mapped by direct acoustic measurements from 6.2% (GEBCO_2014 30-arcsec grid) to 15% (GEBCO_2019 15-arcsec grid just released). Seabed 2030 has four Regional Centers that compile bathymetry data for their areas and a Global Center that produces the global GEBCO grid. The South and West Pacific Ocean regional data centre (SaWPaC) based in Wellington is coordinated by the Technical Management Committee comprised of representatives from NIWA, GNS Science and LINZ. One of the key goals of Seabed 2030 is to identify areas where bathymetric data coverage already exists but is not yet included in the global GEBCO grid. The next step will be to provide the decision support for marine survey agencies by highlighting unmapped areas that could be covered by future research cruises, fishing and industry ship transits. The project remains a global challenge that can only be accomplished through international partnership.
6751: Marine heatwaves (MHWs) pose an increasing threat to the ocean’s wellbeing as global warming progresses. In this study we demonstrate a causal link between ocean heat content and the area and intensity of MHWs in the Tasman Sea on interannual to decadal time scales. Using data from a forced global ocean sea-ice model, we show that ocean heat content fluctuations in the Tasman Sea are predominantly controlled by oceanic meridional heat transport from the subtropics, which in turn, is mainly characterized by the interplay of the East Australian Current and the Tasman Front. Variability in these currents is impacted by wind stress curl anomalies north of this region, following Sverdrup’s and Godfrey’s ‘Island Rule’ theories. Data from models and observations show that periods with positive upper (2000 m) ocean heat content anomalies or rapid increases in ocean heat content are characterized by more frequent, larger, longer and more intense MHWs on interannual to decadal timescales. Thus, the oceanic heat content in the Tasman Sea acts as a preconditioner and has a prolonged predictive skill compared to the atmospheric state (e.g., surface heat fluxes), making ocean heat content a useful indicator and measure of the likelihood of MHWs.
6752: Biosecurity 2025 is a partnership between people, organisations, Māori, and central, local and regional government. Its aim is to make our biosecurity system more resilient and future-focused to protect our taonga and New Zealand from pests and diseases. Since the last New Zealand Marine Science Society conference, a lot of progress has been made on Biosecurity 2025. An implementation plan has been developed, and marine biosecurity has been recognised as being a ‘critical focus area’. The Ko Tātou public campaign has also been launched, with a dedicated website and resources for all to use. This session will provide an update on what’s been happening – from the international stage to what’s been happening across the biosecurity system to improve outcomes.
6753: Parasites are important components of natural systems and among their various roles, strongly influence the flow of energy between and within food webs. Over 1000 tapeworm species are known to parasitise elasmobranchs (sharks, skates and rays), although full life cycles are resolved for fewer than 10 of them. Molecular resolution of transmission pathways is a next step in understanding the role of hosts and parasites within food webs. We investigated the parasite assemblage of New Zealand’s rough skate, Zearaja nasuta. Skates and their prey items (obtained from the skates’ stomachs) were dissected for the recovery of adult and larval tapeworms, respectively. The 28S rDNA region was amplified for all worm specimens to confirm species identity of parasites and to uncover trophic transmission pathways between rough skates and their prey. We identified seven species of tapeworms infecting skates. Four trophic transmission pathways were resolved, i.e. a genetic match was found between larval tapeworms in prey and adult worms in skates. These findings contribute to our limited understanding of cestode life cycles as well as providing insights into the importance of predator-prey relationships for parasite transmission.
6754: At fine scales, the distribution and availability of prey is thought to be more important in shaping a predator’s distribution than characteristics of the physical environment. However, sampling prey is difficult and biotic variables are often overlooked, or add little value, in species’ distribution models. In Fiordland, analyses of habitat use by bottlenose dolphins (Tursiops truncatus) have, until now, focussed on abiotic predictors. We attempt to understand the role of potential prey in the distribution of bottlenose dolphins within Doubtful Sound. We collected data on dolphin distribution during 61 boat-based visual surveys in 2018. Concurrently, baited underwater video (n=307 deployments) was used to collect data on the relative abundance of reef fish. Generalised additive models were used to relate dolphin presence to a suite of predictor variables. Models containing both abiotic and prey variables (deviance explained=36.1%) performed considerably better than models containing abiotic variables alone (deviance explained=19.8%). The top model indicated the probability of finding dolphins was highest at high relative abundance of girdled wrasse, low abundance of tarakihi, and 200m from the coastline. Our results provide important insights into what drives the habitat use of bottlenose dolphins in Doubtful Sound, which will be useful for managing this endangered population.
6755: Disease is one of the greatest threats to shellfish aquaculture and is increasingly recognised as a significant threat to wild shellfish populations. In the aquaculture industry, regular testing has generated knowledge of pathogens and an ability to mitigate losses. The same cannot be said for wild populations, especially species that do not constitute a commercial fishery. Since 2012, Rickettsia-like organisms (RLOs) have been observed while investigating mass-mortality events in at least nine New Zealand shellfish species. In 2017, RLOs were observed in toheroa (Paphies ventricosa) for the first time. Toheroa, a once abundant surf clam, has failed to recover from unsustainable harvesting despite protections. Factors contributing to this failure are currently under investigation, but the role of disease remains a mystery. This study will examine the spatial and temporal distribution of RLOs and other pathogens to determine their contribution to the continued decline of toheroa. We will also ask the question, how can this information be used in a conservation context? Here, we strive to deliver meaningful recommendations for future recovery efforts of an iconic, taonga (treasured) species by considering disease alongside customary management.

6756: Macrofaunal assemblages in soft-sediment environments frequently contain species, ecosystem engineers, that exert a disproportional influence on the structure and diversity of benthic communities. The present study examined the influence of co-occurring but antagonistic burrowing shrimps (Callianassidae) and intertidal seagrasses (Zosteracea) on the diversity of benthic assemblages in two temperate regions, south-eastern New Zealand and north-western United States. In each region, diversity and abundance patterns of intertidal macrofaunal assemblages were examined in relation to varying burrowing shrimp and seagrass densities across different-sized estuaries, in summer and winter. Although the compositions of macrofaunal assemblages were distinctly different between sites dominated by burrowing shrimp and seagrass, differences in univariate assemblage indices were less distinct. While species diversity was generally similar at burrowing shrimp and seagrass sites, species abundance was frequently higher at the latter sites. These patterns were consistent across summer and winter, and across spatial scales, although there were some differences across regions. Even though population densities of burrowing shrimp and seagrass can vary over time, findings from this study highlight the relative influence of these antagonistic ecosystem engineers on the long-term structure and functioning of intertidal macrofaunal assemblages.
National Institute of Water & Atmospheric Research Ltd (NIWA); School of Biological Sciences, Victoria University of Wellington
6757: Tetrodotoxin (TTX) is a highly potent neurotoxin. It is the causative agent in puffer fish poisoning and was originally thought to only occur in puffer fish. It has now been identified in 12 classes of marine, freshwater and terrestrial vertebrate and invertebrate organisms, including marine bivalves. Despite being one of the most studied biotoxins worldwide, the origin of TTX remains a mystery with both exogenous and endogenous sources proposed. The main hypothesis is that Gammaproteobacteria, specifically Vibrio and/or Pseudomonas species, produce TTX and are then ingested by bivalves. This study focuses on Paphies australis, an endemic clam from NZ that has been shown to contain TTX. Paphies australis were collected from ten regions around NZ and analysed for toxin concentration, and P. australis known to contain high TTX concentrations from one site (Hokianga Harbour, Northland) were collected and analysed for TTX concentrations every month over one year. The P. australis were then dissected and the DNA extracted from their digestive glands and siphons, that have previously been shown to contain TTX. Using high-throughput sequencing, we explored how changes in microbial communities from the sediments, the digestive tracts and siphons were related to shifts in TTX concentrations in P. australis.
6758: Bonamia exitiosa (a haplosporidian parasite) is responsible for recurring mortality in Bluff oysters and associated fishery declines. Accurate prediction of where and when mortality from disease is likely to occur is required to inform fisheries management. In addition, the recent discovery of pathogenic, non-native Bonamia ostreae in other regions of New Zealand presents a biosecurity threat to native and farmed oysters, necessitating an effective surveillance programme to detect and contain the spread of infection, and to distinguish between introduced and endemic Bonamia species. We have developed a multiplex ddPCR assay capable of detecting, discriminating and quantifying both Bonamia infections in oysters. It is used for B. exitiosa quantification in Foveaux Strait fisheries stock assessments and for biosecurity surveillance of B. ostreae across a broader region. The assay enables better understanding of the time-scale of disease progression within oyster populations and ensures that B. ostreae can be detected at low infection levels, allowing for early mitigation. In addition to providing information for disease modelling and biosecurity, the multiplex ddPCR assay will also be used to examine the frequency and dynamics of co-infections of B. exitiosa and B. ostreae, which are known to occur but are of unknown significance.
6759: Natural CO₂ vents are increasingly being used as mesocosms to investigate species and community level responses to ocean acidification (OA). Recently, reduced pH around CO₂ vents at White Island, Bay of Plenty, has been suggested to increase the prevalence of algal turfs on surrounding reefs, which has consequences for reef functioning. However, the spatial extent of these impacts has not been quantified. To investigate the effect of the “acidified” environment on benthic communities we mapped vent plumes using geotagged benthic photo surveys accompanied with SeaFET pH data and characterized benthic communities around CO₂ vents at White Island using expanding radius surveys (0.5-3 m). The pH of vent plumes was highly localised and variable. Benthic communities were characterised by heterogeneous mosaics of kelp, fucoid, and turf dominated areas, which were not clearly related to vents. Epifaunal assemblages from turfing algae differed with sampling distance and this was driven by higher Foraminifera and lower bivalve abundance immediately adjacent to vents where sulphur-reducing bacteria were prevalent. Our results contrast previous reports and demonstrate a highly heterogeneous reef and vent environment where it is difficult to separate effects of reduced pH. Future OA research at White Island should carefully consider this spatial variation.
6760: The proposed Kermadec–Rangitāhua Ocean Sanctuary would protect a large, unique, near pristine section of New Zealand’s marine environment, but the proposal has stalled, despite increasing evidence supporting the uniqueness of the region’s species assemblages. Recently, over 150 cephalopod specimens were collected from the Kermadecs during a biodiversity survey (TAN1612), providing the first opportunity in over a century to directly assess locally occurring taxa in this group. Collected specimens were identified to 43 species, using integrative taxonomy (morphology + DNA barcoding); 28 of these were new records for the region, bringing the known cephalopod biodiversity of the Kermadecs to at least 70 species. Several taxa appear badly in need of revision, including some supposedly monotypic genera that now appear to contain multiple species, and at least six species that may be new to science. The Kermadec region thus contains habitats used by more than half of New Zealand’s total reported cephalopod diversity, including 34 species not presently known to occur elsewhere within our Exclusive Economic Zone. Most taxa reported herein are deep-sea species whose habitat is largely unprotected by the existing marine reserve; we therefore strongly support the establishment of the proposed Sanctuary.

6761: The recent introduction of the biofouling Mediterranean fanworm, Sabella spallanzanii, to New Zealand has created concerns for the Greenshell mussel aquaculture operations in the Hauraki Gulf. The fanworm is now well established in many parts of the country, especially around ports and sheltered harbours, where it is capable of colonizing all types of structures. The aim of this study is to examine the settlement behaviour and growth of the Mediterranean fanworm in the context of Greenshell mussel farms in the Coromandel area and learn more about their general biology in northern New Zealand conditions. The reproductive behaviour and seasonality of fanworm has been a particular focus of the study, with the intention to support the development of potential mitigation strategies for this unwanted species. Preliminary results indicate that most worms from a body size of 10-15 cm produce a constant supply of gametes of varying sizes all year round. This variation in gamete size suggests weak synchronicity between individuals spawning, reducing the likelihood of having one particular spawning event or season. This might be one of the reasons why this marine invasive species is so successful and spreads quickly in New Zealand waters.
6762: Characterizing habitat suitability for a marine predator requires an understanding of the environmental variability over the range in which an individual moves during a particular life cycle. Female California sea lions (Zalophus californianus) are central‐place foragers and are particularly constrained while provisioning their young. During this time, habitat selection is a function of prey availability and rookery proximity, which has implications for reproductive and population success. We explore how lactating females may select habitat and respond to environmental variability over broad spatial and temporal scales within the California Current System. We combine remotely sensed satellite oceanography, animal tracking data (n = 72, 2003–2009) and Generalized Additive Mixed Models (GAMMs) to determine the probability of occurrence based on environmental covariates. Results indicate that sea lion presence is associated with cool (<14°C), productive waters, shallow depths, increased eddy activity, and positive sea‐level anomalies. Predictive habitat maps generated from these biophysical associations suggest winter foraging areas are spatially consistent in the nearshore and offshore environments, except during the 2004–2005 El Niño event. We show how a species distribution model can provide information on the distribution of female California sea lions during an important life history stage and its implications for spatial management.

6763: In April 2015 the intra-cellular bacteria New Zealand rickettsia-like organism (NZ-RLO) was detected for the first time in farmed Chinook salmon, Oncorhynchus tshawytscha. These salmon were experiencing clinical signs of disease and mortalities of up to 70% during the summer months. This study presents the detection, phylogenetic analysis, distribution, and pathogenicity of NZ-RLO. Three strains of NZ-RLO were identified using the internal transcribed spacer region and 16S rRNA gene. These strains were specific to certain regions where Chinook salmon are farmed. Two of these strains were associated with clinical signs of disease and found in areas where mortalities occurred. Infectivity trials were carried out and both strains were shown to cause clinical signs of disease and mortalities in Chinook salmon smolt, however the two strains showed differences. This study strongly suggests that certain NZ-RLO are involved in mortalities in farmed Chinook salmon, however elevated temperatures are likely to have amplified the mortalities.
Ministry for Primary Industries; Massey University
6764: Baited remote underwater video (BRUV) may provide valuable data for investigating the efficacy of MPAs and the complex relationships among species, habitat and fishing pressure. We aimed to determine the utility of BRUVs for conducting research on fish populations at Banks Peninsula. In 2017, we made 134 deployments across the two, type 1 MPAs and three nearby control areas. The relative abundance of blue cod and blue moki were compared inside and outside of MPAs and species distribution modelling (SDM) undertaken to determine links between fish distribution and habitat characteristics. Blue moki and blue cod (above minimum size limits) were more abundant in the two MPAs compared to the control areas. SDMs revealed blue cod were more common in deeper habitat dominated by cobble and coarse sediment and blue moki were associated with greater depth and algal dominated communities. Data on fish relative abundance from the BRUVs were useful at investigating spatial relationships among protection strata and with habitat types. A long-term monitoring programme has been established to track changes in the fish community over time in response to variable fishing pressure and habitat patch characteristics allowing new insights into effective MPA design for South Island communities.
University of Otago; Department of Conservation
6765: A series of unprovoked shark attacks on New South Wales beaches between 2013 and 2015 triggered an investigation of new and emerging technologies for protecting bathers. Traditionally, bather protection has included several methods for shark capture, detection and/or deterrence but has often relied on perceived environmentally-damaging techniques. Heightened environmental awareness, including the important role of sharks in the marine ecosystem has seen a demand from the public for new techniques for protection against shark attack. Recent advances in drone, shark capture and tracking technologies have enabled the possibility of real-time shark capture and detection and alerting for public safety. Here we provide an overview and research results for SMART drumlines, drones and the tagging and tracking component of the NSW Government’s Shark Management Strategy.
6766: Pollution is a significant risk to elasmobranch species that inhabit coastal and estuarine waters. Since sharks and rays are thought to take up metals at higher rates than teleost fishes they are arguably more at risk of the bioaccumulation of these elements. Heavy metals, primarily mercury, lead and cadmium (but also copper, chromium and zinc) are biotoxic at high concentrations and are known to negatively affect aspects of physiology (respiratory, reproductive, sensory and musculatory systems) and sometimes behaviour. Consequently, pollution may have direct or indirect impacts on, population viability, species diversity and the functioning of an ecosystem. In this study we examine contaminant body burdens in the New Zealand stingray species Myliobatis tenuicaudatus and Bathytoshia brevicaudata. Sampling was conducted in Tauranga and Porirua Harbours and along the Bay of Plenty coast to test the hypothesis that stingrays occupying more urbanised environments will have higher metal body burdens. Myliobatis tenuicaudatus from both harbour habitats had significantly higher concentrations of Chromium and Lead but significantly lower concentrations of Arsenic than individuals caught in coastal waters. The highest mercury concentration was found in B. brevicaudata from Tauranga Harbour.
National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research
6767: This year, the New Zealand Marine Studies Centre (University of Otago) undertook to develop a ‘Fishy Web Cam’, thanks to funding from the Dunedin GigCity Community Fund. The idea is to use live streaming as some replacement for the public Aquarium that closed in 2012 due a low earthquake rating. The NZ Marine Studies Centre provides education programmes, citizen science projects, production of marine resources, and is constantly scoping for ways to continue to connect the wider community with the marine environment. The Fishy Web Cam project is the first of its kind in NZ to be live streaming the underwater world. Days in the life of Otago Harbour and southern NZ coastal waters will be beamed into classrooms and living rooms, via cameras installed in tanks, off the jetty, and in the labs. This smart technology will provide a easy-to-access window into the sea to highlight the diversity and behaviour of marine wildlife to a wide audience. The project also provides a new set up for marine investigations and research. Data collection of real time environmental variables, alongside the web cameras, provide opportunities to investigate changes and responses in biotic assemblages, over short and longer-term time scales.

6768: New Zealand’s historically largest fishery, the Southern Scallop Fishery (SCA 7) has declined dramatically over the last 16 years from an annual catch of 540 tonnes (meat weight) to the point where it has been closed since 2016 to all fishing to protect the remaining scallop beds. In the absence of fishing, scallop numbers are starting to increase in some parts of the fishery, but not in others. It is likely that factors in addition to fishing, such as disease, turbidity and predation could be contributing to the depression of scallop recovery in these areas. A collaborative process is underway bringing together scientists, industry, government fisheries managers, Iwi and recreational fishers, with the aim of developing an approach that would allow sustainable fishing in the future without compromising this rebuild. Designing an approach to manage catch in this fishery is likely to be challenging, given the potential for localised overfishing and the dynamic nature of scallop populations. There are a number of research projects that could assist us in making more informed management decisions for the benefit of both the fishing community and the marine environment.
6769: Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) are key tools in addressing shark and ray declines, with various “marine parks” and “shark sanctuaries” established to conserve shark populations. There is also a rapidly growing body of telemetry research used to assess MPA performance in shark protection. However, assessments of MPA efficacy in shark protection are often compromised by inconsistent terminology, a lack of standardised approaches, and ambiguity about integrating movement data into assessment processes. This study presents a conceptual framework that standardises key terms and uses the economic concept of Portfolio Risk to fully describe how an MPA may contribute to shark and ray conservation. The framework also demonstrates how movement data can be integrated into the process, and presents seven key questions that provide guidance for applying the framework. Understanding an MPA’s contribution to shark and ray protection requires explicit consideration of the assessment scope, MPA type and purpose, the range of existing and potential threats, the species biophysical attributes and vulnerability, and management and operational contexts. Ultimately, MPA contributions to shark and ray conservation differ according to a complex set of human and natural factors and interactions which should be carefully considered in MPA design, implementation and evaluation.

6770: Ecological assessment is increasingly required by management regulations to quantify the impact of stressors on estuarine and coastal systems. In this presentation, multivariate analysis of community composition at a national scale is proposed as a standardised and sensitive approach to assessing the effects of two stressors (mud and heavy metal contamination) on estuarine health. Benthic macrofaunal data collected at sites across New Zealand were used in separate canonical analyses of principal coordinates to create Benthic Health Models (BHMs) of the responses of macrofaunal community composition to mud content and metal environmental gradients. In addition to being sensitive to changes in ecosystem health, biotic indices need to be unaffected by different species pools and natural environmental contexts. Accordingly, we tested whether estuarine physical type and regional location affect the index values produced and found that the models were suitable for application in two widespread estuary types and across most regions of New Zealand. We also discuss how this national approach relates to assessments carried out at finer scales (regional and estuary) and demonstrate the application of these models using New Zealand case studies. This approach will enable coastal managers across NZ to track health of their estuaries at relatively low cost.
National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research
6771: Since its discovery in 1976, the Megamouth shark (Megachasma pelagios) has remained an enigmatic species. With only ~100 specimens encountered, most of our understanding of this species is based on studies of deceased specimens. Little is known about the behavior or movement patterns of Megamouths. The species is theorized to comprise a single population with global distribution. Information on population structure and movement patterns is needed to best manage the species. This study investigated Megamouth movement by attaching long term pop-off satellite archival tags to three specimens off Taiwan in the Philippine Sea during the summer 2018. Two tags have transmitted data, 66 days from a 565 centimeter female, and 242 days from a 410 centimeter mature male, with the third tag (437 centimeter female) programmed to transmit in November 2019. We tested for short-term area fidelity, preferable habitat conditions, and the potential of prey based migration. Diurnal vertical migration, light levels, and temperature were studied, as well as water depth, proximity to upwelling, and other oceanographic factors that might contribute to an annual migration. Summer aggregations in Taiwan might make Megamouths vulnerable to fisheries, therefore, an understanding of their movements is vital for focused conservation efforts.
6772: Our environment operates at many different scales and has innumerable intricacies and interdependencies. Two of the environment’s most significant and complex systems are climate and oceans. Both systems intimately effect how we live, make a living as well as the things we value. It is for this reason that climate and oceans are a part of the work programme of many government agencies, and science an integral input into these programmes. Alison will outline the importance of connecting across government to ensure best effects in these significant and complex areas, as well as the value of trusted and clearly communicated science to inform decisions. She will also explain the formation and role of the Forum of Chief Science Advisors (convened by the PMCSA) in working together to ensure a more joined up approach across government, and one that that incorporates a credible science voice.
6773: Since human settlement in New Zealand the coastal marine area has undergone modification of marine ecosystems. The extent of human impact and the effect on individual species is often unknown or inferred from unreliable historical data. New Zealand provides a unique opportunity to investigate the impact of human settlement due to its relatively recent occupation and the availability of well-preserved material from archaeological sites throughout the country. The present study compared fish tissue from ancient and modern time points to investigate changes in trophic level and the proportion of alternative organic matter sources (phytoplankton and kelp) through time. This was accomplished using stable isotope analysis paired with mixing models to translate carbon and nitrogen stable isotope signatures into trophic level and relative contribution of phytoplankton to diet. Three time points, six coastal fish species and two regions were selected for study to determine both regional differences in temporal patterns and the response of different species to human settlement. Results demonstrate changes in trophic position among species and between regions. These data provide an important baseline for understanding the changing role of coastal fish species in coastal ecosystems.

6774: To date, genetic monitoring of Hector’s and Māui dolphins has relied on standard DNA profiling, including mtDNA haplotype, sex and up to 25 microsatellite loci. To enhance the power of genomic monitoring, we are using double-digest, restriction-enzyme associated DNA (ddRAD) sequencing. Libraries for ddRAD sequencing were prepared from biopsy samples collected from Māui dolphins in 2015-2016 and sequenced with an Illumina HiSeq 3000 (150 bp, paired-end). We used strict filtering criteria to identify 1,591 variable loci in the Māui dolphin. With these, we confirmed the identity of n = 48 Māui dolphins previously identified by microsatellite genotyping, and the resulting abundance estimate of N = 62 individuals (95% CL, 55 to 73) using a closed population model. Epigenomic monitoring has included a trial study of age-correlated methylation levels at over 30,000 sites in the Māui and Hector’s genomes using a custom hybridisation array. This will enable the future development of an ‘epigenetic clock’ calibrated with known-age individuals for use as a tool to age dolphins from our DNA register and new biopsy samples. Further analyses are underway to estimate effective population size and to identify parent-offspring pairs with ordinal aging for improved estimation of both census and effective population sizes.

6775: Access to live animals for research is a significant factor limiting seafood research in New Zealand and worldwide. Hatchery-based culture of live animals represents a means to access live, undamaged, rested fish populations, to explore all the life stages of a species, and investigate the diverse characteristics of the animal, which are commonly masked by capture damage and fatigue. To realise these opportunities, Plant and Food Research have been investigating the culture of blue cod or rawaru (Parapercis colias). As a coastal species more common in the cooler temperate South Island, blue cod are highly valued by iwi, the commercial and recreational fishing sectors. This popularity, and the increasing pressures faced by the species, create a need to increase our understanding of this endemic finfish. We present an overview of the successes and challenges associated with the development of blue cod in a hatchery environment, and describe aspects of the project, including the collection of gametes, larval development phases, growth and maturation of the species. Potential opportunities for this species are briefly discussed.

6776: Fisheries scientists and managers have historically relied on various fishery dependent and independent data sources to conduct stock assessments, bycatch estimates, and other ecological analyses. Often, these data sources are generated from logbooks, fisheries observer reports, and other paper formats that might take as much as a year or more to be made available for analysis, in some cases resulting in science and management recommendations that are effectively obsolete upon publication. Recently, several emerging technologies as diverse as satellite remote sensing, electronic data capture devices, and artificial intelligence have vastly improved the ability to effectively and efficiently provide more accurate and timely information for use in fisheries conservation and management. This presentation will identify current and future opportunities for the application of innovative and emerging technologies currently employed and under consideration for use in fisheries monitoring, control, and surveillance that will also provide significant improvements in data available for fisheries conservation and management. These technologies, and the information they will provide, have the potential to greatly improve the capacity of fisheries scientists and managers to understand the ecosystems they are responsible for and, in turn, provide better advice for the conservation and management of fisheries resources and the associated ecosystem.
6777: New Zealand is renowned for its rich record of fossil cetaceans. Several undescribed dolphins with “spear-like” horizontally procumbent teeth and long slender jaws have been found in NZ. No extant cetaceans carry such delicate procumbent teeth; however, many fossil species did. These include New Zealand species Waipatia maerewhenua, Otekaikea marplesi, Otekaikea huata (Platanistoidea) and a Kentriodon sp. Specimen (Delphinoidea), as well as Ediscetus osbornei from South Carolina (USA) (Platanistoidea). Other undescribed species with similar tusks have been found in the South Island Waitaki region and are all considered new species. They are known from partial or whole skulls with 6-10 horizontally procumbent apical teeth in their jaws. Two specimens (OU22397, OU22126) have elongate, attenuate, and dorsoventrally flattened rostra, with tusks embedded in elongate premaxillae. The maxillary teeth are polydont; heterodont in OU22397, and near-homodont in OU22126. The periotic (earbone) has a parabullary sulcus, apparently a derived trait for Platanistoidea – superfamily grouping containing the Ganges river dolphin. The function and phylogenetic significance of tusks in fossil dolphins is still uncertain, although feeding or display are possible functions. Understanding the phylogenetic placement of theses specimens will help elucidate the complex evolutionary history of odontocetes.

6778: New Zealand has the 4th largest exclusive economic zone in the world and is a hotspot for marine diversity. However, many of our marine birds and mammals are at risk, and our coastal waters are degraded due to human and natural stressors. Managing the cumulative effects that arise from these stressors is one of the most urgent and complex problems facing marine managers. It is particularly complicated by fragmented legislative regimes and institutions that struggle to deal with cross-scale interactions, chronic data scarcity, and high levels of uncertainty. Concepts such as the ‘precautionary principle’, ‘best available information’ and ‘adaptive management’, have raised the bar in terms of science information needs for decision-makers. As new offshore activities, such as seabed mining, become more feasible, we need to keep bridging the gap between science, policy and practice. Research to improve our understanding of, and management of, the marine environment is occurring through the initiative of the Sustainable Seas National Science Challenge. The Challenge is in a unique position to bring together different stakeholders into various research projects, which has greatly enhanced the uptake of science information by policy-makers and practitioners.
6779: When considering a consent application for the development of a natural resource, the certainty and resolution of information available to a decision maker is largely contingent on the location and spatial scale of the natural resource. The information void in which a decision maker must operate becomes larger the further offshore a resource exists. This is the primary challenge when making decisions under the EEZ Act. One common question asked by regulators, policy makers, and scientists alike is: How can we make robust decisions in a context with information that is low in resolution, and high in uncertainty? Some of the seemingly obvious solutions that are frequently posited are: more data, extrapolation of observations via models, the precautionary principle, and adaptive management. There are factors that limit the application of these solutions, a primary one being that decision makers must decide on applications at a point in time, and base that decision on the best available information. In this presentation I will briefly cover the information puzzle that is decision making in the EEZ, by providing an overview of some of the common issues encountered by decision makers, while applying both marine scientific, and regulatory lenses to this topic.
6780: As natural resource management shifts from government to community-led place-based approaches, we are discovering the importance of creating deeper dialogue between scientist and community. Community participation in environmental monitoring plays a significant role in addressing this issue, allowing resources to be managed at a local scale; enabling community members to regain their roles as guardians of their environment. This aligns with the acknowledgement that multiple forms of environmental data exist, from the numerical results of scientific methods to the traditional ecological knowledge held by kaitiaki. Acknowledging and communicating these different forms data is crucial in effectively managing our ocean, however successful platforms for achieving this thus far are not so well known. This project investigates the potential of ESRI Story Map ArcGIS, ‘Story Maps’ (https://storymaps.arcgis.com/en) to aid place-based management by Tangata Tiaki (Ministerially Gazetted Customary Fishery Managers) in Customary Protected Areas (Mātaitai and Taiāpure). We describe our practice-based research using the East Otago Taiāpure as a case-study. Here, three Story Maps were created to compile and communicate relevant local environmental data. Transmedia, narrative, and ArcGIS mapping were used to communicate Otago University Aquaculture and Fisheries 301 research. The successes and limitations of the platform have been investigated.
6781: Light, substrate and the surrounding community are three important factors in the formation of subtidal biogenic habitats. All three of these were affected by the 2016 Kaikoura earthquake. Initial subtidal surveys showed that sites with high degrees of uplift had extensive areas of bare rock that had been exposed through the underlying sand and gravel. Sparse propagule supply, high turbidity due to erosion of the coastline and high sediment riverine inputs can hinder recovery of these affected areas. Experimental clearance plots were set up to test the effects of understorey algae (corallines, encrusting reds), substrate type (mudstone, limestone) and supply (with and without surrounding large brown algae) on algal recruitment and growth. Laboratory experiments are also being done to evaluate brown habitat-forming macroalgal germling growth in varying temperature, turbidity and light conditions. How algae respond to these varying conditions is important for gauging the recovery of affected Kaikoura habitats and for understanding how algae respond in high turbidity environments that may be human-induced (such as runoff from forestry, and harbour dredging). Algal responses can also be calibrated to a changing climate change of increased temperatures and turbidity.
6782: New Zealand’s coastal and oceanic waters support a valuable seafood sector, which contributes significantly to the country’s annual economy. Significant risks are posed to this sector from CO2- and climate-induced changes to their surrounding environment. We synthesise NZ-specific information on changes in physical and oceanographic parameters projected for the coming decades (including temperature, pH, salinity, oxygen, circulation, etc). We then evaluate the current state of knowledge of how 32 NZ fisheries species, ranging from shellfisheries to inshore, middle-depths and oceanic species, are influenced by these parameters. This information is then used to determine potential risks to these fisheries in the coming decades. Finally, through detailed case studies of paua, snapper and hoki, respectively, we combine scientific data and fisher expertise in an expert evaluation of these species’ vulnerabilities and, importantly, their adaptation potential. Knowledge of how environmental changes might affect different species is essential so that decisions can be made around the potential implications of change to that fishery and the management options available to mitigate them.
6783: Few southern hemisphere time-series measurements of biogeochemical tracers are available, and this scarcity is a major impediment in understanding the processes underlying the oceanic carbon and nutrient cycles in vast parts of the global oceans. The Munida Time series is located off the south east coast of New Zealand in the South Pacific Ocean. At this site, the marine carbon cycle of subantarctic surface waters has been studied since 1998, providing insight into the seasonal, interannual and long term variability of the carbonate chemistry, including ocean acidification. The area is a sink for atmospheric carbon dioxide, and biological activity is the main driver of the pH and pCO2 seasonal cycles, offsetting the effect of changing seawater temperature. A long term increase in pCO₂ of +1.43 μatm/yr, with corresponding decrease of 0.0015 pH units/yr has been observed over the 21 year long time series.
6784: Non-indigenous species have been more frequently observed in New Zealand waters in recent years, as world travel and trade have expanded and diversified. Their impacts on native species, fisheries and local economies is significant. A better understanding of the dynamics of their growth and spread is paramount to predict future patterns and assess the potential effectiveness of control strategies. Here we show the results from stochastic forward simulations, using parameters inputs from a modelling framework which fits to data on positive species observations, probabilities of establishment and growth rates in different habitats, and vessel traffic between major ports (as a potential additional route of transmission). We are thus able to predict species distribution patterns in the future, forecast the effects of altering habitat and climate on this spread, and assess impacts that different management methods can have on population sizes. We thus show for which species eradication from New Zealand is not feasible.
6785: Given the significant challenges facing shark populations globally, improvements for monitoring changes in shark abundance is critical. Populations of marine species are typically monitored using catch-per-unit-effort or capture-mark-recapture surveys as proxies for abundance. However, these methods may not be reliable for detecting trends or change in population size over time, leading to incorrect or incomplete knowledge about the past and present state of a population, to the detriment of management and conservation objectives. The need for alternate methods has led to the increasing use of genetic and genomic markers to evaluate abundance. Here, we use this type of data and population-genetic models to estimate the abundance of breeders in five age-cohorts from a population of white sharks in eastern Australia and compare our results to previous studies. Our intention is to use these genetically-based metrics for long-term population monitoring. We present our insights into the demography of this population, and provide a useful case study for how these methods may be used to monitor other chondrichthyan populations.
6786: The traditional bone fish hooks (matau) as used by the Maori seem, on first impressions, to be fairly inefficient in shape. After making a few copied examples, experiments were carried out in controlled aquarium situations. The technology and design underpinning the hook’s form were explored. The hooks have since been used out in the ‘real world’ and some of the insights gained from creating and using the facsimile hooks will be shared. The work forms the basis of a hands-on education programme offered to school classes in the Nelson/Marlborough regions.
6787: The aim of this study was to assess population attributes of the intertidal gastropod, Amphibola crenata, for use as a bioindicator species to test the effects of trace metal and nutrient contaminants for NZ estuarine habitats. The study was undertaken at 17 estuarine sites across six different regions including Auckland, Canterbury, Nelson, Southland, Waikato and the West Coast. The population structure (e.g. density and/or length distribution) and condition index (CI) of A. crenata were assessed at mid-tide level. The study showed that A. crenata was highly resistant to low levels of certain trace metal contamination including Cu, Zn, Ni, Cd and Pb. The CI of A. crenata was negatively correlated with sediment trace metals (e.g. As, Cd, Cu, and Zn), reflecting potential utility in CI of A. crenata as a biomarker of metal pollution. The study also identified that sediment nutrients played a significant role in determining the structure of A. crenata populations in intertidal areas, supporting the potential use of this species as an indicator of nutrient pollution. The sensitivity of A. crenata population attributes to environmental contaminants, confirmed that A. crenata could be a good bioindicator species to assess the health condition of NZ estuaries.
6788: Multibeam echosounder technology is rapidly becoming the industry and scientific standard for visualising seafloor characteristics and producing habitat maps. The ability to map the sea floor in such detail has many applications in marine spatial management. Here, we describe our approach to benthic mapping and habitat map production. We discuss how this data is being incorporated into the management of customary protection areas and the potential it has for informing ecosystem based management of marine resources.
6789: Measuring animals and quantifying their growth is crucial to answering many ecological questions. Due to their size, whales are inherently difficult to measure. Kaikōura, New Zealand is one of a few places where sperm whales can be studied close to shore. Study undertaken here since 1990 has revealed a decline in this population, mainly driven by fewer whales visiting in summer. This raises the question of whether size structure has changed seasonally, and whether there has been a concurrent trend over time. This study estimated the sizes of whales (n =35) using inter-pulse intervals (IPI) from acoustic recordings gathered over the past four years of field research. Seasonal differences were found in the size structure of this population, with the largest measured whales visiting in summer and smaller whales visiting in winter (t = 2.65, p <0.05). The accuracy of the IPI method will be investigated using very accurate UAV photogrammetry (mean error = 1%) over the next year. Size estimates will also be gathered using acoustic recordings dating back to 1996 to investigate any changes in size structure of this population, and to investigate growth rates among individuals. These results may help explain the ongoing decline in this population.
6790: Estuary soft sediment ecosystems act as a contaminant filter at the land-ocean interface and perform ecosystem functions, such as denitrification, that can provide resilience to increased nitrogen inputs. The nitrogen that fuels estuarine primary production derives from organic matter breakdown in the sediments (a ‘slow’ pathway that generates ammonium-N) and from pulsed inputs following storms (a ‘fast’ pathway delivering primarily nitrate-N). While coupled nitrification-denitrification in sediments is known to reduce pore water ammonium concentrations, little is known about the capacity of sediments to assimilate nitrate-N in the short term after runoff events. Knowledge of the ecosystem attributes that contribute to nitrogen removal processes and the timescales at which they occur is crucial for estuarine ecosystem management. We conducted investigations at four intertidal sites in Mahurangi Harbour, experimentally enriching the water column in benthic incubation chambers simulating a nutrient laden river plume to test whether intertidal habitats can ‘process’ nitrogen from a runoff event. Initial results indicated differences in sediment oxygen dynamics among sites and treatments, suggesting that local biogeochemical processes can respond quickly to increases in water column nutrient concentrations and that there are differences between habitats.
6791: Seabirds are well recognised as indicators of ocean health and productivity. Studying their demographics (breeding success) and foraging behaviour can offer an insight into at sea conditions in addition to signalling a general decrease in ecosystem health. Such measures, however tend to be ‘slow to report’ and a more rapid signal is needed if we are to react in a meaningful way. To this end, ecophysiology offers a potentially rapid insight into current bird health and thus at sea conditions. Using Hauraki Gulf petrels and shearwaters I will highlight key physiological biomarkers that appear sensitive to change within the marine environment. In particular, blood haemoglobin content appears to track the onset of ENSO cycles and weight loss, indicating an upregulation of oxygen delivery in times of stress. Further, by matching these physiological traits with behavioural modelling (Hidden Markov Models) and endocrine responses (corticosterone) a more integrative snapshot of seabird health can be obtained; potentially leading to more effective management. Depending on the foraging range of the study species, the spatial scale “assayed” and reflected in the bird’s physiology can thus reflect the conditions from ocean basins to local council boundaries, thus providing information for a range of differing management jurisdictions.

6792: Isotopic ecology has been widely used to understand spatial connectivity and trophic interactions in marine systems, but comparisons over long time periods are rare. Preserved specimens from museum collections are valuable sources of tissues, but isotopic signatures are known to be affected by fixatives. The aim of this study was to generate a correction factor for the effects of fixatives on carbon and nitrogen isotopes of bulk fish muscle, also to analyse specific amino acid isotopic signatures. Two specimens of Parapercis colias, Seriolella brama and Oncorhynchus tschawytscha underwent formalin fixation and alcohol preservation and were sampled at different time periods. Using AICc and BIC, the best model explained 80% of the isotopic variation due to fixatives, independent of preservation time. Carbon isotopes of amino acids were not affected by treatments. Although nitrogen was significantly affected by fixatives, relationships among amino acids were constant. We applied our findings to reef fishes from Otago, collected between 1950 and the 2018. While trends showed by herbivorous fish are likely related to recent changes in the nitrogen cycle and CO2 inputs to the system, shifts in trophic level and resource use were linked to changes in habitat and stock size of important commercial species.

6793: Investigating the distribution of apex predators is essential for understanding their habitat requirements and can provide insights into community ecology. In New Zealand, only 11 of at least 113 chondrichthyan species are actively managed, emphasising the need for further research. The data deficient broadnose sevengill shark Notorynchus cepedianus is commonly sighted around coastal New Zealand. This study aimed to increase our understanding of their distribution through quantifying habitat selection in Paterson Inlet, Stewart Island. Baited remote underwater videos and associated environmental variables thought to influence shark distribution, were collected during three sampling trips in 2018 (n = 60 deployments). Individual sevengill sharks were identified through unique markings using photo-ID, and the number of sharks observed per deployment was used as an index of relative abundance. Generalised linear models were used to relate relative abundance of sharks to the suite of environmental predictors in a multi-model inference framework. Based on minimum AICc, the best-fitting model (R-squared = 0.69) showed a positive effect of water temperature and salinity, and a negative effect of ambient light. These results provide important insights into the distribution and ecology of sevengill sharks in New Zealand.
6794: A recent risk assessment for chondrichthyans (sharks, rays, and chimaeras) found some deepwater sharks were at relatively high risk of adverse impacts from fishing. Quantitative data for these species is limited, and some available information has been found to be unreliable. With a better understanding of spatial distributions, our knowledge of the risk to, and the status of these species would be more informed. This information would allow for the evaluation of potential stock boundaries, encourage comparisons of New Zealand population structure with populations elsewhere, and overall, better inform fisheries management. Here, we investigate the suitability of vector-autoregressive spatio-temporal (VAST) models, a predictive modelling approach, to estimate spatio-temporal trends for seven deepwater shark species regularly caught in New Zealand deepwater fisheries: Dalatias licha, Etmopterus granulosus, Centroselachus crepidater, Centrophorus squamosus, Deania calcea, Centroscymnus owstoni, and Scymnodon plunketi. Preliminary results from this analysis will be discussed.

6795: Long term population monitoring of the spiny lobster (Jasus edwardsii) within the Cape Rodney to Okakari Point Marine Reserve has shown a decline to pre-reserve numbers. This could potentially be explained by individuals making offshore migrations across the marine reserve boundary, where fishing is permitted. These offshore movements appear to follow after energetically demanding events, such as mating and moulting. Previous laboratory studies have also indicated that these migrations occur at times when captive lobsters are consuming the most food. Therefore, it is hypothesised that lobsters could be making offshore movements in search of energy-rich offshore feeding grounds. To help understand the reasoning behind these offshore movements a grid of sediment grabs were conducted to describe the distribution of potential lobster prey. In conjunction with these findings, different reef and sand prey species were tested in the laboratory for possible feeding preferences and to describe lobster feeding patterns, handling times and energetics. It is hoped that the findings of this study will help policymakers better understand and accordingly protect these vulnerable and valuable species.
6796: In shallow coastal waters, benthic primary producers fuel food-webs and influence nutrient fluxes across the sediment-water interface. Light is an important variable regulating primary production and varies across multiple temporal scales due to weather, tidal stage and season. Additionally, increased delivery of land-based sediments into coastal waters raises water column turbidity reducing photosynthesis. For intertidal habitats, this reduced light availability during immersion may be offset by low tide production. Despite its importance, there is little published data on how light availability influences benthic primary production and associated nutrient fluxes. To rectify this, we seasonally determined photosynthesis-irradiance (P-I) curves and associated nutrient fluxes in seagrass and microphytobenthic (MPB) dominated habitats using benthic incubation chambers deployed at low and high tide with light levels manipulated using shade cloth. Preliminary results indicate comparable production rates during low and high tide for both seagrass and MPB habitats (~4410 vs 4070 & 1280 vs 1010 µmol O₂ m-2 h-1, respectively) confirming the importance of emmersed production. We also saw evidence of photoinhibition at light levels > 360 µmol photons m-2 s-1. Ultimately, the results of this study will help identify light thresholds of benthic primary producers and demonstrate how altering light regimes influences nutrient processing.
6797: Many scientists may wish to influence the behaviour of Fisheries New Zealand. This talk will outline the scope within which Fisheries New Zealand operates, and its key drivers and limitations. This will include the role of science in decision making, and the key processes and opportunities for external input. Some of these opportunities outlined will include how to best discuss research suggestions with Fisheries New Zealand, where to find out about research we are looking to purchase, the role of scientists within Fisheries NZ and participation in our science review processes. Some of the challenges include navigating our procurement and data provision requirements as well as meeting science working group and management application expectations. It is hoped this talk will lead to better understanding of Fisheries New Zealand’s role and processes as well as encouraging people to become involved in these.
6798: The ocean is important to all indigenous Pacific cultures. For Māori, the ocean is an important element of their identity and social belonging. The relationships they have had and continue to have with their maritime environments is symbiotic and symbolically determining. Māori are intimately connected through their atua (deities) and tūpuna (ancestors), and the coast and sea provide sustenance and protection for their whānau (family). This relationship is often in contention with western views and legislative processes toward the marine space and because Māori hold a different perspective toward the marine environment they are often marginalised in decision-making processes. Epeli Hau’ofa’s “re-imagination of the ocean as a highway that links rather than separates” gave prominence to Pacific and seascape epistemology. Thus, this paper will be particularly concerned with highlighting indigenous knowledge, namely mātauranga (Māori knowledge), focusing on west coast communities with a strong connection to Toheroa (Paphies Venticosa), their interaction with the seascape and the tensions faced when negotiating best practice in regards to managing this taonga (treasured) species.
6799: Shark species tend to have low productivity and are therefore vulnerable to over-fishing. This has resulted in management measures that attempt to reduce shark mortality. The Western and Central Pacific Fishing Commission has implemented no-retention measures for some shark species caught on tuna longlines in the Western and Central Pacific Ocean. As a result, many sharks are now released alive. In this study, popup electronic tags were deployed on 60 shortfin mako sharks and 52 silky sharks released from tuna longlines in New Zealand, Fiji, New Caledonia and Marshall Islands. Survival status was determined for over 100 sharks and mortality rates in the first 60 days post-release were estimated for both species. The tags also collected valuable depth and temperature data with which to describe the species’ use of the water column. Displacements between tag deployment and popup locations provided new information on the scale and direction of mako and silky shark movements. Mako sharks showed clear two-way movement between New Zealand and Fiji/New Caledonia.
6800: New Zealand has committed to establishing a representative network of marine protected areas (MPAs). A network of MPAs that represents more of our marine environment will not only have benefits for marine biodiversity conservation but will also be an important scientific resource. To help address known gaps in habitat representation and inform New Zealand’s future MPA strategy, the Department of Conservation (DOC), Fisheries New Zealand and the Ministry for the Environment have been working collaboratively, under an MPA Science Advisory Group, to strengthen the information base to support future MPA planning. Additionally, new funding via DOC’s Biodiversity 2018 Programme has been allocated to a 4-year work stream to develop an improved approach to establishing MPAs. Recent work has been undertaken in conjunction with NIWA to consider how to classify marine and coastal habitats as a foundation for establishing a representative network. Building on this work is the identification of key ecological areas and optimal areas for biodiversity protection, as well as habitats that are under-represented in the current network. Future work will build on these initiatives to support development of sound marine protection policy and more effective approaches to achieving a New Zealand network of MPAs.
6801: This investigation addresses the biological and ecological attributes for 86 species of elasmobranchs mainly distributed in the southern and entrance regions of the Gulf of California. We built a framework in which all elasmobranch species presently distributed within the study regions were identified and arrange taxonomically from the available literature. We selected 48 species of sharks and 38 species of rays with >10% of their distribution. We collated available life history and ecological parameters and we assigned each species to one of four ecological groups (EGs), which is a flexible and novel way to allocate a large number of species based on habitat use, depth strata (shelf-inshore and shelf-offshore), habitat dependence (freshwater, reef substrate, and sandy substrate), and lifestyle (demersal or pelagic). This framework also included four types of fishing: the artisanal fishery, the semi-industrial fishery, the prawn trawl fishery, and the sardine fishery. Two key biological attributes (maximum age and maximum length of each species), four ecological attributes (trophic level, habitat dependence, depth strata and lifestyle), and nine climate change stressors (sea surface temperature, upwelling, salinity, pH, chlorophyll, dissolved oxygen, sea rise level, sea atmospheric pressure, and green gashouses emissions) that affect sharks and rays in the study area.

6802: Based on a growing concern about the impacts of bottom fishing on seabed ecosystems, the United Nations General Assembly has called for the adoption of conservation measures to protect vulnerable marine ecosystems (VMEs). Although spatial management based on open and closed areas present one possible solution, a lack of empirical data on the distribution of VMEs within the high seas means spatial management is often informed by predictions of the spatial distribution of VME indicator taxa. Given the uncertainty associated with these predictions, it is sensible to have a back-stop move-on rule, where fishing vessels are required to move a minimum distance away from locations where VME indicator taxa were encountered. Using bycatch data from 8,850 New Zealand bottom trawls within the South Pacific RFMO Convention Area, we illustrate a data-driven approach for identifying candidate thresholds for triggering move-on responses as a backstop to spatial management measures. We argue that the selection of a final threshold value from a suite of candidate values is a management decision that must balance the sensitivity of the move-on rule with the statistical uncertainty of the modelled distributions of the VME indicator taxa.
Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences
6803: Limited information is available on the fine-scale movements and habitat use of juvenile sharks in very shallow (<1 m) nearshore areas and the factors that drive these behaviours. Active acoustic tracking was used to investigate movements and habitat use of juvenile (683 ± 58 mm TL) blacktip reef sharks (Carcharhinus melanopterus) at Orpheus Island, Australia. Six juveniles were tracked for over 65 hours. Juveniles moved in synchrony with tidal cycles, always remaining within very shallow (<1 m) sandy reef flat or reef crest waters during outgoing, low and incoming tides, and using inundated mangrove habitat during higher tides, indicating tidal fluctuations were a major driver of movement and habitat use. Individuals never entered deep water beyond the fringing reef, restricting their movements within water <60 cm deep. In general, linearity and rate of movement were significantly higher during incoming or outgoing tides, whilst these measures were significantly lower during higher tide heights when juveniles were occupying mangrove habitats. The observed behaviour was most likely a predator avoidance strategy, highlighting the importance of mangrove root habitat use by juvenile blacktip reef sharks in coastal nursery areas indicating this may be an important habitat for the young of this species.
6804: Nearly 3 years after the Mw7.8 Kaikōura earthquake, the coastal ecosystem continues to reassemble and reorganize following massive reef upheaval. Ongoing sampling of algal and invertebrate communities shows that some intertidal reefs are showing encouraging signs of recovery, while others are impeded by rapid erosion, shifting sands, and elevated sea surface and air temperatures during summer months. This instability has challenged the recovery of the black-footed abalone (Haliotis iris or pāua), which require highly-specific under-boulder inshore habitats during early life stages. With customary, recreational and commercial fisheries still under emergency closure in the region, pressure is mounting to understand how these populations are recovering. Here we use extensive field surveys to identify specific habitat requirements for juvenile pāua, quantify habitat availability, and document population demographics through time. We also use surveys and experimental constructed boulder reefs to gauge the results of commercial reseeding of hatchery-raised pāua along the coastline. Finally, we discuss the role that customary management areas and marine reserves may play in recovery following natural disaster.
6805: Blue cod has been one of New Zealand’s most valuable domestic fisheries since the 1930s. The majority of commercial catch is taken by cod potting in Southland and in the Chatham Islands. Blue cod is a significant customary fishery for tangata whenua and the most popular recreational finfish species in the South Island. Fisheries New Zealand has engaged with tangata whenua and stakeholders to develop a National Blue Cod Strategy (the strategy). The strategy was developed in response to increasing concerns from tangata whenua and local communities, about localised depletion of blue cod populations in part due to blue cod’s unique biology. The strategy consists of a set of overarching objectives and management goals to drive a more consistent, integrated and proactive management approach for the blue cod fishery. This approach was overall received positively by the public. Public engagement included public drop-in sessions, a specific website and social media messaging, and the use of online surveys.

Functional diversity is commonly used as a surrogate measure of function, where groups of species with similar functional traits are considered functionally redundant and theoretically buffer against some species loss; but this framework ignores the resistance and recovery capacity of communities that occurs across multiple spatial and temporal scales. We develop a more complete theory of functional resilience to disturbance, linking processes operating across multiple scales of ecological organisation (e.g. individual species tolerances to landscape-scale population connectivity). We explore how different combinations of scale-dependent resilience attributes are linked to functional resilience against disturbances that vary in intensity, spatial-extent, and frequency. 6807: Anecdotal evidence describes the presence of large Macrocystis pyrifera (M.pyrifera) kelp forests along the southern Otago coastline which are now no longer present. There are many different hypotheses why these kelp forests have disappeared but most attribute the loss to an increase in sedimentation in coastal waters due to the downstream effects of gold mining, agriculture, industrialisation, and urbanisation. Anecdotes describe kelp forests that supported Jasus edwarsii, Haliotis iris, Evechinus chloroticus and Odax pullus. Anecdotal evidence such as this, has been shown to be important for inferring historical conditions when there are no long term data sets available. 6808: Recruitment overfishing, whereby adult spawning stock is so depleted a population can no longer replenish itself, is a serious issue for a number of fisheries worldwide. Maintaining spawner biomass is essential to population sustainability, as simply put, sexually immature individuals cannot reproduce. Novel management schemes are needed to conserve large breeding animals and a combination of harvest slot limits and marine protected areas is one potential solution. Using the iconic, and economically valuable Caribbean spiny lobster, Panulirus argus as our model organism we demonstrate the potential for harvest slot limits and MPAs to rebuild and maintain mature populations throughout the Caribbean. To do so, we used a combination of laboratory experiments that examined reproductive output and clutch quality relative to lobster size, and mathematical modelling of different harvest scenarios. We also investigated the possible effect of increasing the abundance of large lobsters in a population, on other species of value. The results, which demonstrate a positive relationship between size and clutch quality highlight the importance of large lobsters to population sustainability. Furthermore, modelling clearly demonstrated the potential for harvest slot limits and MPAs used in concert, to guard against recruitment overfishing at a range of fishing intensities.
